--- title: "Ten Datasets Against UMAP and t-SNE" subtitle: "Default maps win on MNIST-like digits and collapse on moons and shells, and neither method has a loss that could have said so in advance" description: "PCA minimizes a reconstruction error whose value is comparable across settings. UMAP and t-SNE minimize a graph objective they rebuild from the same settings being tuned, so no loss can choose a setting or flag a bad map. On ten canonical clustering datasets, default UMAP and t-SNE score anywhere from chance to near-perfect, and the ranking flips between datasets." author: "Ravi Kalia" date: "2026-11-22" categories: [Machine Learning, Statistics] image: "./cover.png" tags: [UMAP, t-SNE, PCA, clustering, dimensionality reduction, hyperparameters, adjusted Rand index] jupyter: umap-tsne-blog resources: - requirements.txt format: html: toc: true number-sections: true code-fold: true execute: warning: false --- ![Ten Datasets Against UMAP and t-SNE](./cover.png) This post compares default UMAP and t-SNE with PCA on ten labeled clustering datasets, so the reader can see how much a reported grouping depends on the method that drew it. A UMAP plot is easy to believe. Points gather into islands, the islands sit apart, and the eye supplies the conclusion: these are groups. The same picture appears when the grouping is an artifact of `n_neighbors=15`, because the picture carries no number that says which it is. ## The missing loss PCA minimizes squared reconstruction error over all rank-$k$ subspaces. The target is fixed by the data, so every implementation returns the same subspace, and the error is comparable across runs. - **PCA**: minimizes squared reconstruction error, a quantity that means the same thing before and after a setting changes. - **t-SNE**: minimizes KL divergence between pairwise similarities in the original space and in the map. Original-space similarity depends on perplexity, so changing perplexity changes the target. - **UMAP**: minimizes fuzzy-set cross-entropy against a neighborhood graph. The graph depends on `n_neighbors` and the metric, so changing either rebuilds the target. Only PCA has a loss whose value survives a change of settings. A t-SNE run at perplexity 5 and one at perplexity 50 minimize two different objectives, and neither reports a number that makes one preferable. There is no reconstruction error to hold data out against, and no dev-set score with a fixed target to pick a setting. The usual clustering workflow — fit on train, pick settings on dev, confirm on test — needs a target that stays put while settings change. UMAP and t-SNE do not supply one, so the workflow is never run, and plots are read with the confidence it would have earned. ## Ten datasets Four sets are real and labeled: iris (Fisher's 1936 measurements of three iris species), wine (178 Italian wines, three cultivars), breast cancer (Wisconsin diagnostic, two classes), and digits (1,797 8×8 handwritten digits, ten classes — the same task as MNIST at lower resolution). They load from scikit-learn's bundled loaders; nothing is fetched at render time. A wrong grouping here is a wrong subgroup in a biological or clinical dataset. Six sets are synthetic, generated by `sklearn.datasets` with a fixed seed. Three are Gaussian mixtures: well-separated blobs, blobs with unequal variance, and blobs pushed through a random linear map. Two are non-convex — two moons and two concentric circles — standing in for groups a linear projection cannot keep apart. One is concentric Gaussian shells, standing in for nested structure with no obvious cluster count. Embedding to 2-D and running k-means with the known class count gives an adjusted Rand index (ARI) for each map. ARI is 1 for a perfect match and 0 for chance agreement, so a convincing plot with tangled labels scores near zero. The labels are used only to score the map; none of the three methods sees them. ::: {#fig-ari .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} rows = {} for name, (X, y) in DATA.items(): rows[name] = { "PCA": ari(PCA(n_components=2, random_state=SEED).fit_transform(X), y), "t-SNE": ari(TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=SEED, init="pca").fit_transform(X), y), "UMAP": ari(umap.UMAP(n_components=2, random_state=SEED).fit_transform(X), y), } results = pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3) display(results) names = list(results.index) x = np.arange(len(names)) width = 0.26 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.2)) for i, (method, colour) in enumerate( zip(["PCA", "t-SNE", "UMAP"], ["#4c72b0", "#dd8452", "#55a868"]) ): ax.bar(x + (i - 1) * width, results[method], width, label=method, color=colour) ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8) ax.set_xticks(x) ax.set_xticklabels(names, rotation=30, ha="right") ax.set_ylabel("Adjusted Rand index") ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05) ax.legend(ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.12), frameon=False) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {#fig-ari-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
PCA t-SNE UMAP
iris 0.620 0.630 0.611
wine 0.895 0.788 0.774
breast cancer 0.659 0.649 0.779
digits 0.326 0.771 0.861

``` Adjusted Rand index of k-means on each 2-D embedding. Zero is chance agreement with the labels. UMAP and t-SNE run at library defaults; PCA uses two components. ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/fig-ari-output-2.png){#fig-ari-2} ::: ::: No method wins, and the ranking flips between datasets: - PCA leads on wine, 0.895 against 0.788 for t-SNE and 0.774 for UMAP. UMAP leads on breast cancer, 0.779 against 0.659 for PCA. - On digits, UMAP reaches 0.861 and t-SNE 0.771, against 0.326 for PCA. This is the one setting where the nonlinear methods look miraculous. - t-SNE's default perplexity of 30 scores 0.002 on moons, chance agreement, while UMAP scores 0.586 on the same points. On circles, UMAP scores 1.000 and both PCA and t-SNE sit at 0.000. - All three sit at chance on Gaussian shells: 0.007, 0.001, and 0.002. None of the three embeddings carries a value that predicts this ordering. The only number a reader gets is the picture. ## Every setting is valid Change `n_neighbors` or `min_dist` in UMAP, or perplexity in t-SNE, and the map changes without ceasing to be a valid output of the algorithm. Because the objective is rebuilt from those settings, none of the resulting embeddings can be rejected by the loss that produced it. ::: {#settings-sweep .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} X, y = DATA["wine"] mds = [0.0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.99] nns = [5, 15, 50, 100] display(pd.DataFrame( [ [ round(ari(umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=nn, min_dist=md, random_state=SEED) .fit_transform(X), y), 3) for md in mds ] for nn in nns ], index=pd.Index(nns, name="n_neighbors"), columns=[f"min_dist={md}" for md in mds], )) X, y = DATA["iris"] display(pd.Series( { p: round(ari(TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=p, random_state=SEED, init="pca").fit_transform(X), y), 3) for p in [5, 10, 30, 50] }, name="ARI", ).to_frame()) ``` ::: {#settings-sweep-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Sixteen UMAP settings on wine score between 0.774 and 0.852; on iris, t-SNE scores between 0.610 at perplexity 50 and 0.818 at perplexity 10. The spread is wide enough to change a conclusion, and every value in it is a legitimate run. There are as many defensible settings as there are values to try. Changing only the seed does the same thing. ::: {#cell-seed-sweep .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} X, y = DATA["moons"] display(pd.Series( { s: round(ari(umap.UMAP(n_components=2, random_state=s).fit_transform(X), y), 3) for s in range(6) }, name="ARI", ).to_frame()) ``` ::: {#seed-sweep .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
ARI
0 0.586
1 0.593
2 0.565
3 0.580
4 0.996
5 0.524
``` ::: ::: Six UMAP runs on moons at otherwise identical defaults score between 0.524 and 0.996. One seed finds a near-perfect separation; the others merge the arcs. With no labels there is no way to tell the lucky run from the usual one, and UMAP's own objective does not rank them. ## Why MNIST fooled everyone Digits is the showcase: ten balanced classes, 64 features, 1,797 samples, and clear separation between digit shapes. It is the closest thing here to MNIST, and it is the dataset on which UMAP and t-SNE look best — 0.861 and 0.771 against PCA's 0.326. Papers illustrate these methods on exactly this kind of data, so the defaults are calibrated for a regime most clustering problems do not have. Wine has 178 rows and three classes that overlap in feature space. Breast cancer has two classes separated by a handful of features. Moons and circles have two dimensions. On all of them the default map is a guess about scale, neighborhood size, and density that the method cannot check, and on moons the guess lands at chance. ## Constraints ARI on a 2-D map is one proxy, not a verdict on the method. Clustering in the original space, or choosing a metric that fits the data, can change every number above; ARI also rewards methods that happen to preserve the class count. The point is not that PCA is always right — it scores 0.000 on circles — but that PCA's failure has a known cause in a linear projection, while a bad UMAP or t-SNE map has no loss that names it. Plots. Convince. Nothing. Checks. Endless. Knobs. Defaults. Guess. Trust. Nobody. ## References - McInnes, L., Healy, J., & Melville, J. (2018). [UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426). - van der Maaten, L., & Hinton, G. (2008). [Visualizing Data using t-SNE](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v9/vandermaaten08a.html). - Pedregosa, F., et al. (2011). [Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python](https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/pedregosa11a.html). - Fisher, R. A. (1936). [The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-1809.1936.tb02137.x). - [scikit-learn dataset loaders](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/datasets/toy_dataset.html).
